final_proof:
Let \(X\) be a set and let \(\Sigma\subseteq\mathcal P(X)\) be a \(\sigma\)-algebra. We show that union restricts to a binary operation on \(\Sigma\), which makes \(\Sigma\) a magma of sets.

By definition, \(X\in\Sigma\), \(\Sigma\) is closed under complements relative to \(X\), and \(\Sigma\) is closed under countable unions. In particular,
\[
\varnothing=X\setminus X\in\Sigma,
\]
so \(\Sigma\) is nonempty.

Now let \(A,B\in\Sigma\). Define a sequence \((E_n)_{n\ge 1}\) by
\[
E_1=A,\qquad E_2=B,\qquad E_n=\varnothing\quad(n\ge 3).
\]
Every \(E_n\) belongs to \(\Sigma\). Therefore, by closure under countable unions,
\[
A\cup B=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}E_n\in\Sigma.
\]
Thus ordinary set union defines a map
\[
\cup:\Sigma\times\Sigma\longrightarrow\Sigma.
\]
A magma is a nonempty set equipped with a binary operation. Hence \((\Sigma,\cup)\) is a magma, and since every element of \(\Sigma\) is itself a set, it is a magma of sets. Therefore every \(\sigma\)-algebra is an instance of a magma of sets.
